To describe a city and the memories attached to it.
Sunday, 27 April. Hélène has asked Ioana and Julien to take her for a walk around the neighbourhood of her youth, Croix-Rousse. She walks slowly, with her stick, but her eyes are full of light.
Do you see this yellow building? It’s the building where I grew up. On the third floor, the window with the flowers.
That’s two streets from us! You lived so close?
Yes. My father was a silk weaver, like many people who lived here. He wove silk all day long.
And Henri, where did you meet him?
Come, I’ll show you. (They go into a dark corridor.) It’s a traboule. The silk weavers used it to carry the silk without getting wet.
It’s magical! You go right through the buildings!
And here’s the little square where Lucette’s café used to be. That’s where we met every Thursday.
No, it’s a chemist’s now. But the bench where we used to sit is still there. Look!
What did you do on Thursdays?
Henri told me about the music he was composing, the concerts he dreamt of. What impressed me was his passion.
Did he study at the conservatoire?
Yes, the one on the banks of the Saône. He was the best student in his class. The day he played my waltz at the end-of-year concert, the whole hall cried.
Is that the memory you’re proudest of?
Perhaps. But do you know what I like best today? This bench, this sun, and two young people listening to an old lady.
“Qui” = “kee”, with a clear i. “Que” = “kuh”, with a short “uh”. You can clearly hear the difference: “l’homme qui” vs “l’homme que”.
“Où” (where) is pronounced exactly like “ou” (or): “oo”. Only the grave accent tells them apart in writing.
“Dõ”, with a nasal o, as in “bon”. The final t is silent.
“Tra-bool”: a Lyon word, from the Latin “trans-ambulare” (to walk through).
“Noo noo-za-say-YÕ”: the imperfect of s’asseoir. Liaison with z after the first nous.
Both can translate “who / which / that”, but they have different roles. QUI is the subject of the verb that follows. QUE is the direct object; another subject comes after it.
the man who plays the piano
Quick test: after QUI comes a VERB straight away (qui joue). After QUE comes a SUBJECT (que Julien joue, que je préfère).
“Que” becomes “qu’” before a vowel: “la musique qu’il composait”. “Qui” is NEVER shortened: “l’ami qui arrive”, not “qu’arrive”.
In the passé composé, the past participle agrees with the noun before “que”: “la lettre que j’ai écrite”, “les photos que nous avons prises”.
“Où” replaces a place, like English “where / in which”. But French also uses it for TIME, where English says “when / on which”:
The building where I grew up.
The day (when) he played my waltz…
The year (when) I arrived in Lyon.
For time, you DON’T use “quand” after a noun: “le jour où” (not “le jour quand”).
“Dont” replaces a complement introduced by “de”. It is used above all with verbs and expressions that take “de”:
le jour dont je me souviens
le souvenir dont je suis fière
“Dont” also expresses possession, like “whose”: “Madame Bernard, dont le mari s’appelait Henri…” (Madame Bernard, whose husband was called Henri…).
When there is no noun before it, French uses “ce”: ce qui (subject), ce que (object). They are often used to highlight something:
What impressed me was his passion.
What I like best is this bench.
Do you know what I mean?
In a direct question you say “Qu’est-ce que tu veux ?”, but in an indirect one “Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.” (not “qu’est-ce que”).

On 3 May, as Julien had promised, there was a party in the flat in rue d’Austerlitz. It was Hélène’s birthday: she was eighty-four.
Sophie had made the cake. It was a cake in the shape of a piano, with keys in white and dark chocolate. There were eighty-four candles. It took three people to light them.

Madame Bernard had arrived first, with a big box. In the box were all the photos of Henri she had kept: Henri on his ship, Henri in New York, Henri in Tokyo, Henri with his daughter Isabelle on his shoulders.
The two women settled on the sofa, the box between them. Hélène looked at each photo for a long time. “It’s the man I knew,” she said softly, “and at the same time, it’s a man I never knew.”

Madame Bernard told her about the journeys Henri always talked about, the countries he had been to, the languages he had learnt. Hélène, for her part, told her about the young student who composed waltzes on a bench in Croix-Rousse.
Together they were piecing together the life of a man they had both loved, forty years apart. What amazed Ioana was that there was no jealousy between them. Only tenderness.

Paul Martin, the painter, had brought a present. It was a drawing he had made from memory: Lucette’s café as it was in 1960. “I used to go there to buy sweets when I was little,” he explained. Hélène cried with joy.

Then Julien sat down at the piano and played the waltz. This time everyone knew it. Karim whistled it, Leïla danced with her daughter, and Madame Bernard asked Hélène to dance. The two old ladies took three steps, then laughed so hard that they had to sit down.
At about ten, Ioana’s phone rang. It was her mother, Elena, calling from Iași. Ioana put it on speaker.
“Good evening! I can hear music! Is that the party you told me about?” asked Elena in her school French.

“So, this Julien you talk about all the time… is he really coming in July? Your father has already bought the wine. And your grandmother is drawing up the list of things he has to taste. It’s very long.”
Everyone laughed. Julien came over to the phone. “Good evening, Elena! Yes, I’m coming. It’s the trip I’ve been dreaming of for months.”
After the call, Hélène winked at him. “A grandmother drawing up a list… My poor Julien. The things you’re going to eat!”

That night, when everyone had left, Ioana found a little note on the piano, written in a slightly trembling hand: “Thank you for the most beautiful birthday of my life. The piano is at last in the home Henri promised me. Hélène.”

Croix-Rousse is a hill that overlooks Lyon. It is called “the hill that works”.
In the 19th century it was the district where the canuts lived, the workers who wove silk.
The buildings you can see have very tall windows. They let in the light the silk weavers needed to work.
In 1831 the canuts, who earned very little, rose up. It’s a story Lyon people are still proud of.
What makes the neighbourhood charming today is its traboules, its stairways and its big market on the boulevard.
Don’t miss the Maison des Canuts, a small museum where you’ll see a real loom.
And end your visit at the Gros Caillou, a huge stone with a magnificent view over the city and the Alps.
